title: What’s going on in this picture?

fn.en: Describe paintings; speculate and make deductions.

gr: must, might, could and can’t for deduction

can.en: I can say how sure I am about something I cannot know for certain.

acts.say: Say which of these you would trust as evidence.

cols.en: 🔍 You can see it in the picture

sub.en: You cannot know. How sure are you, and what is your evidence?

items.q: People are skating on it, so the river ___ frozen.
items.why: must = I am almost certain, and I can point to the evidence.

items.q: They ___ going out to hunt — I can see they have already caught something.
items.why: can’t is the opposite of must for deduction. mustn’t means “it is forbidden”, which is different.

items.q: It ___ a picture of an old story, but I am not sure.
That shape ___ be a window. Actually, no — it’s a mirror.
It ___ painted recently. Look at the clothes.
items.why: For a past deduction, use must / might / can’t + have + past participle.

items.q: The artist ___ seen the real place — the detail is too exact.
It ___ have been painted in winter, or the artist imagined the snow.
This is ___ the most detailed painting in the room.

lines: People are skating on it, so the river [must be|can be|might not be] frozen.
They [can’t be|mustn’t be|couldn’t have] going out to hunt — they’ve already caught something.
That shape [could|must|can’t] be a window. Actually, no, I think it’s a mirror.
It [can’t have been|mustn’t be|couldn’t be] painted recently — look at the clothes.
The artist [must have|must had|must be] seen the real place; the detail is [far|by far|much most] too exact.

items.why: For deduction the negative of must is can’t. mustn’t means “it is forbidden”.
can is not used for a positive deduction. Use must for what you are almost sure of.

tts: I love this painting because it’s so detailed, and it really tells a story. The colours are quite soft — mainly white, brown and a kind of blue-green.
It’s a landscape, and it must be either an old painting or a painting of a historical scene.
In the bottom left-hand corner there are some men with dogs. I think they might be going out to hunt. Ah, no — they can’t be going out to hunt, because I can see they’ve caught something.
Just to their left there’s a group of women doing something with a big fire. I’m not sure exactly what they’re doing. They could be cooking something.
It all looks very cold. There’s lots of snow on the ground and on the mountains in the distance.
The river must be frozen over, because people are skating on it in the valley towards the right-hand side.

items.q: Why does the speaker change her mind about the men?
o: She can see they have already caught something
She sees they have no dogs

items.q: How sure is she about what the women are doing?
o: Not sure — she says they could be cooking
She says it is impossible to guess

items.q: What is her evidence that the river is frozen?

tts: I think this painting is really beautiful. It’s a portrait of a woman.
She’s wearing an old-fashioned long dress in a bright shade of red, with a purple scarf. There’s the same red on her lips and on the side of the book in front of her.
She’s drinking from a blue glass bowl. I have no idea why — it’s really mysterious. It might be a picture of an old story or something.
The woman is in the foreground of the picture, but the background is also really detailed.
Behind her there’s a curved window. No, actually, it can’t be a window. I think it must be a mirror. It’s reflecting the sea and two old-fashioned sailing ships.
I’d love to know what this picture is actually about.

items.s: The painting is a portrait of a woman.
The speaker knows exactly why the woman is drinking from the bowl.
She first thinks the curved shape is a window.
She concludes that it must be a mirror.
The background of the painting has almost no detail.

items.sit: People are skating on the river and you are almost certain why.
They have already caught something, so one explanation is impossible.
You have an idea, but you are far from sure.
o: It might be a scene from an old story.
It might to be a scene from an old story.
It must be maybe a scene from an old story.

items.sit: The clothes make a recent date impossible.
o: It can’t have been painted recently.

items.sit: The detail is so exact that you are almost certain the artist was there.
o: The artist must have seen the place.
The artist must had seen the place.
The artist must be seen the place.

items.sit: You want to give a soft opinion rather than a firm deduction.
o: I’d say it’s probably a mirror.
I’d say it’s probably to be a mirror.
I’d say probably it is a mirror to be.

write.q: Choose a photograph or a picture you can see right now — on your wall, on your phone, in the street. Describe what is definitely there, then say what you deduce from it. Use must, might or could, and can’t at least once each, and one past deduction with must/might/can’t + have.
plan: what is definitely in the picture
one thing you are almost sure of + why
one thing that is impossible + why
write.model: In the foreground there are two men on a bench outside a shop, and in the background a bus that is not moving. Both men are wearing heavy coats, so it must be winter, or at least very cold. It can’t be early morning, because the shadows are long and coming from the left. One of them is holding a bag of something warm — I’d say it’s probably bread, from the shape. They might be waiting for the bus, but neither of them is looking at it, so perhaps they are simply sitting. Whoever took the photograph must have been standing in the road, which is the part I find hardest to explain.

speak.q: Describe the same picture out loud to somebody who cannot see it. Say what is there, then what you deduce, and make your level of certainty clear each time.
speak.model: In the foreground there are two men on a bench, and behind them a bus that isn’t moving. They’re both in heavy coats, so it must be winter. It can’t be early morning — the shadows are long and coming from the left. One of them is holding something warm; I’d say it’s probably bread. They might be waiting for the bus, but neither of them is looking at it.
